kurals.tamil:
வஞ்ச மனத்தான் படிற்றொழுக்கம் பூதங்கள்
ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vanja manaththaan padittrozhukkam boodhangal
Aindhum agaththe nagum.
kurals.meaning: When a man with a deceitful mind puts on a false show of holy conduct, the five elements that make up his own body laugh at him from within.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone pretending to be very good while secretly cheating. People outside might be fooled, but the earth, water, fire, air and sky that his body is made of can see everything — and they giggle at the silly act. You can’t hide a lie from the stuff you are made of.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a striking image: the five great elements (pancha bhutas — earth, water, fire, air, ether) that compose the hypocrite’s body are themselves the witnesses who see through his sham piety and laugh inwardly. The word படிற்றொழுக்கம் (padittrozhukkam) denotes counterfeit or disguised conduct, and அகத்தே (agaththe) plays on “inside” — both inside the body and inside themselves. The point is that concealment is metaphysically impossible: the deceiver carries his witnesses with him. Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the elements’ laughter as mockery of a man who thinks he can fool the world while his own substance knows the truth — a theme paralleled by Manu’s list of cosmic witnesses and the Qur’anic image of skins testifying.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The wicked, indeed, say in their hearts, ‘Nobody sees us;’ but the gods distinctly see them and the male within their own breasts. The sky, the earth, the waters, (the male in) the heart, the moon, the sun, the fire, Yama and the wind, the night, the two twilights, and justice know the conduct of all corporeal beings.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells witnesses that no one lies unseen: the sky, earth, waters, fire, wind and the inner self are all watching everything a person does.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same list as the Kural’s five elements: the physical world itself is the witness that knows the hypocrite’s real conduct.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structurally (elements as witnesses of hidden conduct); Manu’s context is courtroom perjury rather than false asceticism, and the elements ‘know’ rather than ‘laugh’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples against hypocrisy and says that whatever is hidden will eventually come out into the open.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats religious pretence as ultimately transparent: what the hypocrite hides is already known.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on the futility of concealed hypocrisy; lacks the elemental-witness and mockery imagery.

islam.quote_or_event: “Until, when they reach it, their hearing and their eyes and their skins will testify against them of what they used to do.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement, the Qur’an says a person’s own body parts — ears, eyes, skin — will speak up and report what that person did.
islam.tie_back: The same idea as the Kural: the hypocrite’s own body is the witness against him.
islam._accuracy_note: Near match on ‘one’s own body as witness’; eschatological setting, and testimony rather than laughter.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him… Whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs describes a person who hides malice behind pleasant words and says his wickedness will eventually be exposed publicly.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that a deceitful inner life cannot stay covered; exposure and shame follow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on hidden deceit being exposed; not specifically about religious pretence or elemental witnesses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever being depraved, devoid of self-control and truthfulness, should don the monk’s yellow robe, he surely is not worthy of the robe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a person who is corrupt and untruthful gains nothing by wearing a monk’s robe — he simply does not deserve it.
buddhism.tie_back: Names the exact sin of the chapter — holy dress over a deceitful mind — though without the image of the elements mocking him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Precise match on the subject (false ascetic), weaker on the Kural’s specific image of inner witnesses laughing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the song of Demodocus, Aphrodite and Ares carry on a secret affair in Hephaestus’ house; Helios the Sun, who sees everything, reports it, Hephaestus traps them in an invisible net, and the assembled gods burst into laughter at the exposed pair.
greek_mythology.explanation: A hidden wrongdoing is seen by a cosmic power (the Sun), exposed, and met with the gods’ mocking laughter.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s picture of a natural, all-seeing element exposing concealed misconduct and laughing at it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: shares ‘elemental witness + laughter at hidden misconduct’, but the offence is adultery, not religious hypocrisy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld observes that hypocrites pretend to be good precisely because goodness is admired; their disguise is a backhanded compliment to virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Diagnoses the same phenomenon the Kural mocks — vice dressed up as virtue — with a similarly ironic, laughing tone.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the ironic view of hypocrisy; does not include the idea of inner witnesses.

kurals.tamil:
வானுயர் தோற்றம் எவன்செய்யும் தன்னெஞ்சம்
தான்அறி குற்றப் படின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaanuyar thotram evanseyyum thannenjam
Thaanari kutrap padin.
kurals.meaning: What good is an appearance of holiness as high as the sky, if a man’s own heart is sunk in faults that he himself knows about?
kurals.elementary: Suppose you wear a shiny superhero costume, but inside you know you just took your friend’s toy without asking. The costume doesn’t make you a hero. What you know about yourself matters more than how you look.
kurals.university: வானுயர் தோற்றம் (“a sky-high appearance”) refers to the imposing garb and bearing of the ascetic, and Valluvar poses a rhetorical question: of what use is it? The criterion he sets is not public exposure but self-knowledge — தன்னெஞ்சம் தான் அறி குற்றம், the fault the heart itself is aware of. Valluvar thus locates moral judgement in conscience rather than reputation, a remarkably interior standard for an ancient ethical text. The kural parallels the Gita’s notion of mithyācāra (the pretender whose mind dwells on what his outward restraint pretends to renounce), and Stoic ideas of conscience as the one witness who cannot be deceived.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses and organs of action, but whose mind dwells on sense objects, certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that someone who outwardly acts restrained but inwardly keeps craving is a mithyācāra — a fake.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s case: impressive outer discipline is worthless when the heart knowingly clings to what it pretends to have given up.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: outward austerity versus inward indulgence, labelled hypocrisy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things.”
christianity.explanation: John says that when our own heart accuses us, God — who knows even more than our heart — sees the whole truth.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the decisive verdict comes from the heart’s own knowledge of its guilt, not from outward appearance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘self-condemning heart’ theme; the Johannine context is assurance before God rather than critique of sham asceticism.

islam.quote_or_event: “Rather, man, against himself, will be a witness, Even if he presents his excuses.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says each person is a witness against himself and knows the truth about his own deeds, whatever excuses he offers.
islam.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘fault the heart itself knows’: no outward show can override inner self-knowledge.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on self-witness; lacks explicit mention of religious costume.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me…”
judaism.explanation: God complains through Isaiah that the people honour him outwardly with words while their hearts are elsewhere.
judaism.tie_back: Same gap the Kural exposes — splendid outward devotion, empty or guilty heart — and the same verdict that the outward form is worthless.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on outward devotion versus inner distance; Isaiah speaks of a nation, not an individual ascetic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The evil-doer suffers here and hereafter; he suffers in both the worlds. The thought, ‘Evil have I done,’ torments him…”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the wrongdoer is tormented by his own awareness of what he has done.
buddhism.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s focus on the self-known fault as what really counts, whatever the outward show.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the self-aware guilt theme; does not address outward holy appearance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After killing his mother, Orestes is hounded by the Furies (Erinyes) — spirits of guilt and vengeance whom he cannot escape even at Apollo’s shrine, until he is tried before Athena’s court.
greek_mythology.explanation: Orestes’ protected status at a holy place cannot silence the pursuit of his guilt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, sacred surroundings and status do not neutralise a known wrong; guilt follows the doer.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best mythic parallel: guilt that holy status cannot remove; Orestes is not a hypocrite and his act was divinely commanded.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If your deeds are honourable, let everybody know them; if base, what matters it that no one knows them, as long as you yourself know them? How wretched you are if you despise such a witness!”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius that hiding a shameful act is pointless, because you yourself are always a witness to it.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost Valluvar’s exact point: reputation is irrelevant when the self knows its own fault.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 43.5 (tr. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on self-knowledge as the true witness; not specifically about ascetic dress.

kurals.tamil:
வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம் பெற்றம்
புலியின்தோல் போர்த்துமேய்ந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Valiyil nilaimaiyaan valluruvam petram
Puliyinthol porththumeindh thatru.
kurals.meaning: A man without the inner strength to master his senses who puts on the stern appearance of an ascetic is like a cow grazing on crops while wrapped in a tiger’s skin.
kurals.elementary: Picture a cow wearing a tiger costume so it can sneak into a farm and eat the crops. It looks scary, but it’s still just a cow munching grass. A person who dresses like a strong holy person but can’t control himself is the same — a costume on the outside, the same old habits inside.
kurals.university: The simile is doubly pointed: the cow is weak, not fierce, and the tiger-skin lends it a borrowed terror that lets it graze unchallenged on another’s field. வலியில் நிலைமையான் (“one lacking the strength” — traditionally, strength to restrain the senses) contrasts with வல்லுருவம் (“a mighty form”), the forbidding garb of tapas. The target is not ordinary weakness but the exploitation of a sacred appearance to feed appetite. The same fable circulated widely in the ancient world — the Panchatantra’s ass in the tiger-skin and Aesop’s ass in the lion’s skin — and in both the disguise ultimately betrays itself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra story “The Ass in the Tiger-Skin,” a washerman dresses his donkey in a tiger’s skin and turns it loose in the farmers’ fields at night; everyone flees from the ‘tiger’ while it eats the grain, until it brays and is recognised and killed.
hinduism.explanation: A weak animal wearing a fearsome skin feeds on others’ crops until its real voice gives it away.
hinduism.tie_back: This is essentially the Kural’s image told as a story — the borrowed skin, the grazing on crops, and the inevitable exposure.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book 4, “The Ass in the Tiger-Skin” (tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical image (herbivore grazing crops in a tiger skin); the fable is a general moral tale rather than a critique of false ascetics.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns of religious teachers whose gentle outward appearance hides a predatory nature.
christianity.tie_back: The same animal-disguise logic as the Kural, inverted: here the predator wears the harmless skin, but in both the costume misrepresents the real creature.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on disguise imagery and religious impostors; direction of disguise is reversed (predator as sheep vs. cow as tiger).

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up…”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes hypocrites whose impressive outward forms hide inner hollowness, like dry timber propped up to look solid.
islam.tie_back: Like the tiger-skinned cow, the hypocrite’s imposing exterior has nothing strong behind it.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on impressive exterior vs. inner weakness; lacks the element of feeding on others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not be afraid of the Pharisees, and neither [should you fear] from those who are not Pharisees; rather, beware of the hypocrites who appear like Pharisees, as their actions are like the act of the wicked Zimri and they request a reward like that of the righteous Pinehas.”
judaism.explanation: King Yannai warns his wife that the real danger is people who look like pious Pharisees but act like sinners while demanding a saint’s reward.
judaism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s type: someone borrowing the appearance of the devout while their deeds belong to a weaker, baser nature.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 22b (William Davidson / Koren–Steinsaltz translation)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on religious disguise masking base conduct; no animal simile.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are many evil characters and uncontrolled men wearing the saffron robe. These wicked men will be born in states of woe because of their evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that plenty of undisciplined people wear the monk’s robe, and their robe will not save them.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘weak in self-control but strong in appearance’ figure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Precise match on uncontrolled men in holy garb; no animal image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “An Ass found a Lion’s Skin, and dressed himself up in it. Then he went about frightening every one he met… Elated by the success of his trick, he loudly brayed in triumph.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The ass in the lion’s skin scares everyone until its own braying reveals what it really is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek twin of Valluvar’s simile: a weak animal in a predator’s skin, exposed by its true nature.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, “The Ass in the Lion’s Skin” (tr. V. S. Vernon Jones)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-identical disguise image; Aesop’s ass seeks to frighten, not to graze crops, and the fable is not about religion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The boastful man, then, is thought to be apt to claim the things that bring glory, when he has not got them, or to claim more of them than he has…”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines the boaster as someone who claims admirable qualities he does not possess.
philosophy.tie_back: The tiger-skinned cow is a boaster in Aristotle’s sense: claiming the strength of austerity without having it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptual match on false claims to virtue; lacks the religious and predatory dimensions.

kurals.tamil:
தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல் புதல்மறைந்து
வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thavamaraindhu allavai seydhal pudhalmaraindhu
Vettuvan pulsimizhth thatru.
kurals.meaning: To hide behind the garb of penance and commit wrongs is like a hunter who hides behind a bush to snare birds.
kurals.elementary: A bird hunter hides in a bush so the birds think it’s just a plant, and then — snap! — he catches them. Someone who pretends to be holy so people trust him, and then tricks them, is doing the same thing. The holy look is just his hiding bush.
kurals.university: Valluvar here turns from the hypocrite’s inner weakness to his active predation. The verb மறைந்து (“hiding”) appears twice in parallel — தவம் மறைந்து / புதல் மறைந்து — making tapas itself the thicket, the camouflage that renders the trapper invisible to his prey. The trusting public are the birds (புள்), drawn close precisely because the cover looks harmless and natural. This anticipates the widespread Indian motif of the “cat-ascetic” (baiḍāla-vratika) who adopts vows to lure victims — condemned in both the Mahabharata and Manu — and resonates with Jesus’ charge that the Pharisees ‘for a pretence make long prayer’ while devouring widows’ houses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A wicked cat, O king, once on a time took up his abode on the banks of the Ganges, abandoning all work and with his hands upraised (after the manner of a devotee). Pretending to have purified his heart, he said unto all creatures… I am now practising virtue.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata the ‘ascetic cat’ wins the trust of the mice with a show of austerity and then eats them one by one until an old mouse sees through him.
hinduism.tie_back: A precise match: austerities used as a hiding place from which to trap trusting victims — Valluvar’s hunter in the bush.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 161 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: feigned penance as cover for predation on the trusting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus accuses religious leaders of using long public prayers as a front while cheating vulnerable widows.
christianity.tie_back: Same structure as the Kural: piety as a blind behind which the vulnerable are caught.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in substance; lacks the fowler image.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the hypocrites [think to] deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. And when they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing [themselves to] the people and not remembering Allah except a little.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says hypocrites use prayer as a public display to deceive, while their hearts are not in it.
islam.tie_back: Worship becomes a screen for deception, as tapas does in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches religious practice used as cover; emphasis is on showing off rather than actively trapping others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men. As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit…”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah compares deceivers among God’s people to bird-trappers lying in wait, their houses crammed with loot like a cage full of birds.
judaism.tie_back: Uses the very same fowler-and-birds image as the Kural for those who prey on others from concealment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Striking image match; Jeremiah’s targets are wicked men generally, not specifically false ascetics.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, blazing like fire, than as an immoral and uncontrolled monk to eat the alms of the people.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says an immoral monk living on people’s trusting donations does something worse than swallowing burning iron.
buddhism.tie_back: Condemns the same abuse: living off public trust earned by a religious appearance.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches exploitation of religious trust; no concealment/trap imagery.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Greeks leave the Wooden Horse — presented as a sacred offering — outside Troy; the Trojans bring it into the city, and the warriors hidden inside emerge at night to sack it.
greek_mythology.explanation: An apparently holy gift conceals armed men waiting to strike.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the hunter behind the bush, danger hides inside something that looks sacred and harmless.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: concealment inside a sacred-seeming object; a war stratagem rather than personal religious hypocrisy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Glaucon’s tale, the shepherd Gyges finds a ring that makes him invisible; using it, he commits adultery, murders the king and seizes the throne — Glaucon argues that anyone who could act unseen would do the same.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the ring to ask whether people are just only because they fear being seen.
philosophy.tie_back: The false ascetic’s robe works like Gyges’ ring: it makes his wrongdoing invisible, exactly as the bush hides the hunter.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual parallel on concealment enabling wrongdoing; no religious disguise.

kurals.tamil:
பற்றற்றேம் என்பார் படிற்றொழுக்கம் எற்றெற்றென்று
ஏதம் பலவுந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Patratrem enbaar padittrozhukkam etretrendru
Edham palavum tharum.
kurals.meaning: The false conduct of those who claim, “We have renounced all attachment,” will bring them many sorrows that make them cry out, “What have we done! What have we done!”
kurals.elementary: If you tell everyone you gave up sweets, but secretly eat them all, one day you’ll be caught — and you’ll feel terrible and say, “Why did I do that?” Pretending costs more in the end than being honest.
kurals.university: The kural records the hypocrite’s own claim — பற்றற்றேம் (“we are free of attachment”) — and sets against it his eventual cry, எற்று எற்று (“what [have we done], what!”), an onomatopoeic doubled lament unusual in the Kural. Valluvar’s focus is on consequences: படிற்றொழுக்கம் (disguised conduct) produces ஏதம் பலவும், “many evils,” culminating in bitter self-reproach. The phrase may refer both to worldly ruin when the imposture is exposed and to karmic suffering afterwards. The pattern — pretended renunciation leading to anguished regret — is echoed in Manu’s consignment of ‘cat’ and ‘heron’ ascetics to hell and in Jesus’ ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ for hypocrites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those Brahmanas who act like herons, and those who display the characteristics of cats, fall in consequence of that wicked mode of acting into (the hell called) Andhatamisra.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu says religious pretenders who behave like the ‘cat’ or the ‘heron’ (feigning piety to catch prey) fall into a dark hell.
hinduism.tie_back: Same moral arithmetic as the Kural: sham renunciation leads to great suffering for the pretender.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on consequences of false piety; the Kural stresses remorse, Manu stresses punishment.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, the unfaithful servant is sent to share the fate of hypocrites, a place of weeping and grinding teeth.
christianity.tie_back: The hypocrite’s end is anguished lament — the Kural’s cry of ‘What have we done!’
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on hypocrites ending in grief; context is an unfaithful servant parable.

islam.quote_or_event: “The hypocrites will call to the believers, ‘Were we not with you?’ They will say, ‘Yes, but you afflicted yourselves and awaited [misfortune for us] and doubted, and wishful thinking deluded you…’”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement the hypocrites plead that they were outwardly with the believers, and are told that their self-deception ruined them.
islam.tie_back: Captures the Kural’s scene of the pretender’s too-late realisation that his false show has destroyed him.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the hypocrite’s belated anguish; no explicit claim of renunciation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah describes hypocrites suddenly seized with terror when judgement arrives.
judaism.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s picture of the pretender overtaken by distress and crying out in dismay.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on hypocrites’ sudden dread; not specifically about claimed detachment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as kusa grass wrongly handled cuts the hand, even so, a recluse’s life wrongly lived drags one to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a monk’s life lived falsely injures the one who lives it, like grass grabbed the wrong way slicing the hand.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s warning: the renunciant’s life, when faked, turns against the faker and brings him grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: false renunciation becomes the cause of one’s own suffering.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A Wolf resolved to disguise himself in order that he might prey upon a flock of sheep without fear of detection. So he clothed himself in a sheepskin… But that very night… the shepherd… laid hands on the Wolf in mistake for a Sheep, and killed him with his knife on the spot.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The wolf’s disguise works — so well that it gets him slaughtered as a sheep.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The disguise itself becomes the source of the deceiver’s ruin, as the Kural predicts of false renunciation.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, “The Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing” (tr. V. S. Vernon Jones)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit on self-defeating disguise; a fable, not about religious pretence, and no remorse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A good conscience welcomes the crowd, but a bad conscience, even in solitude, is disturbed and troubled.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says a person living falsely is haunted and uneasy even when alone.
philosophy.tie_back: Describes the inner torment that the Kural’s ‘What have we done!’ expresses.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 43.5 (tr. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the inner-distress consequence; lacks the claim-of-renunciation element.

kurals.tamil:
நெஞ்சின் துறவார் துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nenjin thuravaar thurandhaarpol vanjiththu
Vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
kurals.meaning: There are none more hard-hearted than those who have not renounced in their hearts, yet live by deceiving others while posing as renunciants.
kurals.elementary: Some people pretend to be kind helpers who need nothing, so others trust them and give them things — but secretly they are greedy. Valluvar says that tricking people who trust you like this is about the meanest thing a person can do.
kurals.university: Valluvar’s strongest verdict in the chapter uses வன்கணார் — literally “the hard-eyed,” those without compassion — and makes it superlative: none are worse (இல்). The contrast நெஞ்சின் துறவார் / துறந்தார்போல் (“not renounced in heart” / “like those who renounced”) sharpens the gap between inner reality and outward role. The special cruelty lies in exploiting the reverence and generosity that society extends to genuine renunciants, and so corrupting the very institution of trust. Plato made the same ranking when Adeimantus and Glaucon called seeming-just-while-being-unjust the ‘highest reach’ of injustice, and Manu classes such pretenders as ‘cats’ bent on doing injury.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(A man) who, ever covetous, displays the flag of virtue, (who is) a hypocrite, a deceiver of the people, intent on doing injury, (and) a detractor (from the merits) of all men, one must know to be one who acts like a cat.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes the ‘cat-like’ pretender: greedy inside, flying the banner of virtue outside, deceiving people and bent on harm.
hinduism.tie_back: A point-by-point match: inner craving, outward show of virtue, deceit, and cruelty toward others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: covetous heart, virtuous display, deceit, intent to injure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus closes his denunciation of the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees with his harshest words anywhere in the Gospels.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats religious hypocrisy as the worst category of wrongdoing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the severity of condemnation; does not itself describe the renunciation disguise.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire – and never will you find for them a helper.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an places hypocrites in the very lowest level of Hell, below open disbelievers.
islam.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s superlative judgement: those who feign faith are worse than any other sinners.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel in ranking hypocrites as the worst; different idiom (punishment rather than hard-heartedness).

judaism.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes a betrayer whose gentle words hide a heart set on violence.
judaism.tie_back: Captures the cruelty the Kural sees in soft outward piety covering a hostile, grasping heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on gentle exterior masking cruelty; not specifically about feigned renunciation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by shaven head does a man who is indisciplined and untruthful become a monk. How can he who is full of desire and greed be a monk?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha asks how anyone still full of craving could truly be a monk, whatever his shaved head suggests.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘not renounced in heart yet appearing renounced’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Precise on the heart/appearance gap; lacks the ‘none more cruel’ verdict.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Lycaon receives Zeus (Jupiter) as a guest with an outward show of hospitality, but secretly plans to murder him and serves him human flesh; Zeus destroys his house and turns him into a wolf.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sacred duty — hospitality to a guest — is used as a cover for murderous cruelty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the false renunciant, Lycaon exploits a sacred role to harm the trusting, and is shown to be a beast within.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best mythic parallel: sacred form masking savagery; the sacred role is host, not ascetic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…for the highest reach of injustice is: to be deemed just when you are not.”
philosophy.explanation: In the Republic, Glaucon argues that the perfectly unjust man is the one who does wrong while enjoying a reputation for justice.
philosophy.tie_back: The same ranking as the Kural: the person who does wrong behind a reputation for goodness is the worst of all.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on hypocrisy as supreme wrong; Glaucon states it provocatively rather than endorsing it.

kurals.tamil:
புறங்குன்றி கண்டனைய ரேனும் அகங்குன்றி
முக்கிற் கரியார் உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Purangundri kandanaiya renum agangundri
Mukkir kariyaar udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The world has people who look as bright and red outside as the kundri (jequirity) seed, yet inside are as black as the seed’s dark tip.
kurals.elementary: There’s a tiny seed that is shiny red all over — except for one small black spot. Some people are like that: they look bright and good on the outside, but they hide a dark spot inside. Don’t judge only by the shiny part.
kurals.university: The kundri (குன்றி, Abrus precatorius) is a brilliant scarlet seed with a black spot at its ‘nose’ (மூக்கு); Valluvar makes it an emblem of the hypocrite, crimson-bright in outward piety, black at the core. The line plays on the repeated குன்றி in புறம் (outer) and அகம் (inner) — the fundamental Tamil poetic pair — so that the seed embodies both states at once. The seed was also used as a jeweller’s weight and is poisonous, which adds a latent irony: something small, attractive and valued conceals toxicity. The image anticipates Jesus’ ‘whited sepulchres’ and Hesiod’s Pandora — beauty outside, deceit within.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That Brahmana, who with downcast look, of a cruel disposition, is solely intent on attaining his own ends, dishonest and falsely gentle, is one who acts like a heron.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes the ‘heron’ pretender who keeps his eyes lowered like a meditating saint but is cruel and selfish inside.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kundri seed, the heron-ascetic shows a gentle surface and a dark interior.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on falsely gentle exterior and cruel interior; different emblem (heron vs. seed).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus likens hypocrites to whitewashed tombs — bright outside, full of corruption inside.
christianity.tie_back: The Christian twin of the kundri seed: a beautiful exterior with darkness at the core.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: striking outward/inward colour contrast applied to religious hypocrites.

islam.quote_or_event: “The signs of a hypocrite are three: 1. Whenever he speaks, he tells a lie. 2. Whenever he promises, he always breaks it… 3. If you trust him, he proves to be dishonest.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists the hidden traits by which someone who looks like a believer can be recognised as a hypocrite.
islam.tie_back: Tells us how to find the ‘black tip’ behind the bright exterior: look at speech, promises and trust.
islam._accuracy_note: Relevant diagnostic of hidden hypocrisy; lacks the outer/inner image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares warm, fervent speech covering a wicked heart to a cheap clay pot coated with a silvery glaze.
judaism.tie_back: A shiny surface over something base — the same contrast as the kundri’s red body and black tip.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong image match on attractive coating over inner corruption.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says fine speech and good looks mean nothing if the person inside is envious, selfish and deceptive.
buddhism.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: a fine exterior cannot redeem a dark interior.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on exterior vs. inner deceit; no visual emblem.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Also the Guide, the Slayer of Argus, contrived within her lies and crafty words and a deceitful nature at the will of loud thundering Zeus…”
greek_mythology.explanation: The gods adorn Pandora with beauty and finery, but Hermes places lies and a deceitful nature inside her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Pandora is the mythic kundri seed: dazzling outside, deceit within.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 69–82 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong outer-beauty / inner-deceit image; Hesiod’s myth is misogynist aetiology, not critique of religious hypocrisy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But the affectation of simplicity is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more disgraceful than a wolfish friendship (false friendship). Avoid this most of all. The good and simple and benevolent show all these things in the eyes, and there is no mistaking.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius says pretended goodness is twisted and false friendship is the worst disgrace; real goodness shows plainly.
philosophy.tie_back: Condemns the same split between an appealing outside and a hidden, predatory inside.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the condemnation of affected goodness; different image and social rather than religious context.

kurals.tamil:
மனத்தது மாசாக மாண்டார் நீராடி
மறைந்தொழுகு மாந்தர் பலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaththadhu maasaaga maandaar neeraadi
Maraindhozhugu maandhar palar.
kurals.meaning: Many are the people who, with filth in their minds, bathe in sacred waters as though they were great souls, and live hidden behind that show.
kurals.elementary: Taking a bath gets the dirt off your skin — but it can’t wash away a mean or dishonest thought. Some people make a big show of holy bathing so everyone thinks they’re pure, but inside they’re still dirty. Clean hands don’t mean a clean heart.
kurals.university: Ritual bathing (நீராடல்) was the most visible sign of purity in both Brahmanical and Tamil religious life; Valluvar turns it into an instrument of concealment. The phrase மாண்டார் நீராடி can be read ‘bathing like the great (மாண்டார்)’ — imitating the ablutions of true sages — and மறைந்தொழுகு (‘conduct in hiding’) suggests that the water itself becomes a screen, as Kalaignar’s gloss has it: submerged, the bather disappears. The mind (மனம்) is the site of மாசு (impurity), echoing Kural 34’s definition of dharma as a mind free of stain. Across traditions, from Isaiah’s ‘Wash you, make you clean’ to Heraclitus mocking blood-purification, the same protest is made: outward ablution cannot cleanse inward defilement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha, an old tiger sits “newly bathed on the bank of a pool, like a Brahman, and with holy kuskus-grass in his paws,” offering a golden bangle and assuring a traveller, “I am strict at ablutions and alms”; the greedy traveller wades in, sticks in the mud, and is eaten.
hinduism.explanation: The tiger uses the marks of ritual purity — bathing, holy grass, charity — to lure a victim into his reach.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s figure: ritual bathing performed as a disguise for a predatory mind.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book 1, “The Story of the Tiger and the Traveller” (tr. Edwin Arnold)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: ostentatious ablutions masking a wicked intent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess. Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within…”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says hypocrites wash the outside of the cup while leaving the inside filthy, and tells them to clean the inside first.
christianity.tie_back: The same contrast as the Kural between outward washing and inner impurity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on ritual cleanliness vs. inner defilement.

islam.quote_or_event: “So woe to those who pray, [But] who are heedless of their prayer – Those who make show [of their deeds].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns worshippers who go through the motions of prayer only to be seen.
islam.tie_back: Ritual acts done for display while the heart is absent — the Kural’s showy bather.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on ritual performed for show; ablution not specifically mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And when ye spread forth your hands, I will hide mine eyes from you… your hands are full of blood. Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil.”
judaism.explanation: God tells worshippers that their prayers are rejected because their hands are bloody; real washing means stopping their evil deeds.
judaism.tie_back: Makes the Kural’s point directly: ritual washing is empty without cleansing one’s conduct.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: outward purity and worship vs. inner and practical impurity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha mocks an ascetic who keeps the outward marks and washes his body while his mind is tangled with passion.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: outward cleansing by someone whose mind remains defiled.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: outer cleansing, inner impurity, ascetic context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, Prometheus divides a sacrificial ox: he hides the meat inside the stomach and wraps the bare bones in glistening fat, and invites Zeus to choose; Zeus picks the attractive portion, and ever after the gods receive bones wrapped in fat at sacrifices.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sacred rite is turned into a trick, with a pleasing surface covering something worthless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s bather, religious ritual is used as a cover, its fine surface hiding the reality.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: ritual form used for deception; the deceiver is a trickster-god, and the hidden thing is worthless rather than impure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They vainly purify themselves by defiling themselves with blood, just as if one who had stepped into the mud were to wash his feet in mud. Any man who marked him doing thus, would deem him mad.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus ridicules people who think blood-rituals can make them pure.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s scepticism that outward purification rites can cleanse real impurity.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, fragments 129–130 (Burnet numbering; tr. John Burnet)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on futility of ritual purification; Heraclitus targets the ritual itself, not hypocrites’ hidden motives.

kurals.tamil:
கணைகொடிது யாழ்கோடு செவ்விதுஆங் கன்ன
வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kanaikodidhu yaazhkodu sevvidhuaang kanna
Vinaipadu paalaal kolal.
kurals.meaning: The arrow, though straight, is cruel; the lute, though its neck is bent, is sweet. In the same way, judge people by the nature of their deeds, not by how they look.
kurals.elementary: An arrow looks perfectly straight, but it’s made for hurting. A guitar has a curvy neck, but it makes lovely music. So don’t decide who is good just by how they look — watch what they actually do.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar moves from condemnation to method: how can one tell the hypocrite from the saint? The paired images turn the usual metaphors upside down — கணை (arrow) is straight yet கொடிது (cruel), while யாழ்கோடு (the curved neck of the yazh, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) is bent yet செவ்விது (upright, good). Since செம்மை and கொடுமை mean both ‘straight/crooked’ and ‘good/cruel’, the kural exploits the double meaning to show that visual straightness and moral straightness are different things. The conclusion — வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல், ‘assess by the quality of deeds’ — is a pragmatic epistemology of character that parallels Jesus’ ‘by their fruits ye shall know them’ and the Yaksha’s answer that conduct, not birth or learning, makes a Brahmin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is neither birth, nor study, nor learning, that is the cause of Brahmanahood, without doubt, it is behaviour that constitutes it.”
hinduism.explanation: Yudhishthira tells the Yaksha that a person is truly a Brahmin by conduct alone, not by birth or scholarship.
hinduism.tie_back: Same standard as the Kural: judge people by their actions, not by outward markers of status.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on conduct over appearance/status; lacks the arrow-and-lute image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?”
christianity.explanation: Right after warning about wolves in sheep’s clothing, Jesus says people are known by what they produce.
christianity.tie_back: Almost identical rule to the Kural’s: ignore the look, judge by the results.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: deeds as the test of character, in a context about impostors.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says God judges by hearts and actions, not by appearance or riches.
islam.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s rejection of appearance as a measure; adds the heart alongside deeds.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on deeds over looks.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi said: don’t look at the container but at that which is in it: there is a new container full of old wine, and an old [container] in which there is not even new [wine].”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that the vessel’s look tells you nothing about its contents.
judaism.tie_back: Like the straight arrow and curved lute, the outward shape misleads; what matters is what the thing really holds and does.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (appearance vs. substance); original context is choosing teachers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even though he be well-attired, yet if he is poised, calm, controlled and established in the holy life, having set aside violence towards all beings — he, truly, is a holy man, a renunciate, a monk.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says someone dressed like an ordinary layperson can still be a true holy man if his conduct is right.
buddhism.tie_back: The ‘curved lute’ case: the wrong look, but the right deeds — judge by conduct.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close: misleading appearance, true character shown in conduct.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns to Ithaca, Athena disguises him as a ragged old beggar; the suitors mock and abuse him, but he is in fact the rightful king, revealed by his deeds when he strings the great bow.
greek_mythology.explanation: A shabby appearance hides a hero, whose true identity is shown by what he does.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The ‘bent lute’ half of the Kural: an unimpressive look that hides real worth, known only through action.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates appearance misleading and deeds revealing; no moral hypocrisy involved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Alcibiades compares Socrates to the statues of Silenus sold in shops — grotesque figures that open up to reveal images of the gods inside — saying that Socrates’ ugly, satyr-like exterior hides divine virtue within.
philosophy.explanation: Plato presents Socrates as proof that an unappealing outside can contain the finest character.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s curved lute: a crooked-looking form that produces something beautiful.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (unpromising exterior, excellent interior); Plato does not add the ‘straight arrow is cruel’ half.

kurals.tamil:
மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும் வேண்டா உலகம்
பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mazhiththalum neettalum vendaa ulagam
Pazhiththadhu ozhiththu vidin.
kurals.meaning: There is no need to shave the head or to grow the hair long, if one simply gives up what the world condemns as wrong.
kurals.elementary: Some holy people shave their heads and some grow their hair really long. Valluvar says: your haircut doesn’t make you good! If you stop doing bad things, you’re already on the right path — hair or no hair.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with its most famous and most radical line. மழித்தல் (shaving the head, as Jain and Buddhist monks did) and நீட்டல் (growing matted locks, as Shaiva and Vedic ascetics did) were the defining visual signs of rival renunciant orders; Valluvar dismisses both in a single breath, declaring them unnecessary (வேண்டா). The only real requirement is ethical: உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்தல் — abandoning what the wise of the world condemn. This non-sectarian move, placing conduct above every order’s insignia, is characteristic of the Kural as a whole and parallels the Dhammapada’s dismissal of tonsure and matted hair, Manu’s ‘the external mark is not the cause of merit’, and Seneca’s warning against the philosopher’s unkempt beard.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…let him, though blemished (by a want of the external marks), fulfil his duty, equal-minded towards all creatures; (for) the external mark (of the order) is not the cause of (the acquisition of) merit.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the renunciant that the outward signs of his order do not produce spiritual merit; right conduct does.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s own claim: ascetic insignia are unnecessary; ethical conduct is what counts.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: external marks of renunciation are not the source of merit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus criticises people who make their fasting visible on their faces so others will admire them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s shaved or matted heads, visible ascetic signs are rejected as mere display.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on rejecting outward ascetic display; does not state the positive rule of abandoning wrongdoing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah… and gives wealth… [and who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; [those who] fulfill their promise…”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says righteousness isn’t about outward ritual forms like the direction you face, but about faith and good conduct.
islam.tie_back: Same move as the Kural: outward religious form is secondary; ethical life is what matters.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on form vs. substance; concerns prayer direction rather than hair or dress.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God…”
judaism.explanation: Joel calls people to real inner repentance instead of the outward sign of tearing their clothes.
judaism.tie_back: Replaces an outward religious gesture with inner change — as the Kural replaces tonsure and matted locks with giving up wrongdoing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on inner reform over outward sign.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by shaven head does a man who is indisciplined and untruthful become a monk.” / “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rejects both tonsure and matted hair as marks of holiness; only truth and righteousness count.
buddhism.tie_back: Names the same two hairstyles as the Kural (shaving and long locks) and reaches the same verdict.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both shaven head and matted hair dismissed in favour of ethical conduct.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women: Vice, dressed and made up to show off her charms, and Virtue, plainly and modestly clothed; Heracles chooses Virtue’s hard road of good deeds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus’ allegory contrasts glamorous outward appearance with genuine virtue shown in action.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells us that real goodness is chosen in conduct, not in how one is dressed or adorned.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: appearance vs. virtue; not about ascetic grooming.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius not to advertise his philosophy through scruffy hair and ostentatious poverty; the real difference should be inward.
philosophy.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: long hair and showy austerity are unnecessary; inner reform is what matters.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 5.2 (tr. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on rejecting ascetic grooming as display; Seneca’s reason is partly social (not repelling others).
